claim: In mammalian cells genes that are in close proximity can be transcriptionally coupled: silencing or activating one gene can affect its neighbors.
source: In mammalian cells genes that are in close proximity can be transcriptionally coupled: silencing or activating one gene can affect its neighbors.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that sets up the research question. It is supported by the subsequent experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Silencing by KRAB, associated with histone methylation, spreads between two genes within hours, with a time delay that increases with distance.
source: We find that silencing by KRAB, associated with histone methylation, spreads between two genes within hours, with a time delay that increases with distance.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data showing delay times between mCitrine and mCherry silencing (Figure 3B&C), and flow cytometry model fits (Figure 3I).

claim: Fast KRAB-mediated spreading is not blocked by the classical cHS4 insulators.
source: This fast KRAB-mediated spreading is not blocked by the classical cHS4 insulators.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing that cHS4 insulators do not prevent spreading of silencing after KRAB recruitment (Figure 4C&D, Figure 4F).

claim: Silencing by histone deacetylase HDAC4 of the upstream gene can facilitate background silencing of the downstream gene by PRC2, but with a days-long delay that does not change with distance.
source: Silencing by histone deacetylase HDAC4 of the upstream gene can also facilitate background silencing of the downstream gene by PRC2, but with a days-long delay that does not change with distance.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 1H&J), CUT&RUN showing H3K27me3 deposition (Figure 2D&E), and EZH2 inhibitor experiments (Figure 2G&H).

claim: HDAC4-mediated slower silencing can sometimes be stopped by insulators.
source: This slower silencing can sometimes be stopped by insulators.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing that cHS4 insulators can attenuate HDAC4-mediated mCherry silencing in K562 cells (Figure 4G&H).

claim: Gene reactivation of neighboring genes is coupled, with strong promoters and insulators determining the order of reactivation.
source: Gene reactivation of neighboring genes is also coupled, with strong promoters and insulators determining the order of reactivation.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing reactivation patterns after CR release (Figure 5B-G) and the observation that reactivation order depends on promoter strength and insulator presence.

claim: The KRAB repressive domain from zinc finger 10 is one of the strongest repressor domains in human cells.
source: The KRAB repressive domain from zinc finger 10 is commonly used in synthetic biology applications (Nakamura et al., 2021), is one of the strongest repressor domains in human cells (Margolin et al., 1994; Witzgall et al., 1994; Cong et al., 2012; Tycko et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KRAB is associated with spreading of heterochromatin and epigenetic memory through positive feedback mechanisms.
source: is one of the strongest repressor domains in human cells (Margolin et al., 1994; Witzgall et al., 1994; Cong et al., 2012; Tycko et al., 2020), and is associated with spreading of heterochromatin and epigenetic memory through positive feedback mechanisms (Bintu et al., 2016; Ayyanathan et al., 2003; Groner et al., 2010; Amabile et al., 2016; O'Geen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KRAB-mediated gene silencing operates through recruitment of cofactors, including KAP1, HP1, and SETDB1, that read and write the repressive histone modification H3K9me3.
source: KRAB-mediated gene silencing operates through recruitment of cofactors, including KAP1, HP1, and SETDB1, that read and write the repressive histone modification, histone 3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3), creating a positive feedback loop that establishes stable gene silencing (Ayyanathan et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Targeted recruitment of the KRAB domain from ZNF10 has been shown to repress gene expression and lead to loss in histone 3 acetylation and gain of H3K9me3 across several tens to hundreds of kilobases.
source: Targeted recruitment of the KRAB domain from ZNF10 has been shown to repress gene expression, and lead to loss in histone 3 acetylation and gain of H3K9me3 across several tens to hundreds of kilobases around the target gene depending on the method and duration of recruitment (Groner et al., 2010; Amabile et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HDAC4 recruitment leads to fast gene silencing, comparable to that of KRAB.
source: We have previously shown that HDAC4 recruitment leads to fast gene silencing, comparable to that of KRAB (Bintu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: KRAB recruitment for 5 days in CHO-K1, K562, and HEK293T cell lines resulted in silencing of both the upstream mCitrine gene and the downstream mCherry gene in the NS and 5 kb reporter lines.
source: Using flow cytometry to measure fluorescence intensity, we observed silencing of both the upstream mCitrine gene and the downstream mCherry gene in the NS (Figure 1C&D) and 5 kb (Figure 1E&F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) reporter lines for the cell types tested.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C-F.

claim: Spreading of silencing upon KRAB recruitment still happens at different dox concentrations in both the NS and the 5 kb reporters.
source: Tuning the probability of KRAB recruitment at the reporter by varying dox concentration, we found that spreading of silencing still happens, in both the NS and the 5 kb reporters, and the percentage of cells with both genes silenced increases with dox concentration (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data at different dox concentrations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: HDAC4 recruitment resulted in silencing of both genes, albeit not in all cells in the population.
source: Surprisingly, HDAC4 recruitment also resulted in silencing of both genes (Figure 1G&J), albeit not in all cells in the population: only 68–78% of CHO-K1 cells silenced mCherry with HDAC4 (Figure 1G&I) compared to 97–100% with KRAB (Figure 1C&E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G-J.

claim: In K562 cells, HDAC4-mediated silencing of mCherry was much slower, taking up to 20 days, compared to 5 days in CHO-K1 cells.
source: Moreover, in K562 cells, HDAC4-mediated silencing of mCherry was much slower, taking up to 20 days, compared to 5 days in CHO-K1 cells (Figure 1H&J).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H&J.

claim: With HDAC4-mediated recruitment at the 5 kb dual reporter in HEK293T at the AAVS1 locus, the majority of cells that silence mCitrine also silence the downstream mCherry within 7 days.
source: With HDAC4-mediated recruitment at the 5 kb dual reporter in HEK293T at the AAVS1 locus, the majority of cells that silence mCitrine also silence the downstream mCherry within 7 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), similar to the CHO-HAC system, and much faster than in K562.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Cellular background can play a strong role in the speed of silencing and spreading.
source: These results suggest that cellular background can play a strong role in the speed of silencing and spreading, as all other factors in the systems are held constant such as reporter set up and genomic locus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that silencing dynamics differ between cell types (CHO-K1, K562, HEK293T) despite identical reporter constructs and genomic loci.

claim: The percent of cells silenced were statistically significant and reproducible for NS and 5 kb reporters in all cell types tested.
source: A Welch's unequal variances T-test comparing the percent of cells off in -dox versus + dox for each gene, showed that the percent of cells silenced were statistically significant (p < 0.05) and reproducible for NS and 5 kb reporters in all cell types tested (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (Welch's T-test) of flow cytometry data.

claim: In CHO-K1 cells in the absence of dox, mCherry expression is lower and has a wider distribution in the 5 kb reporter compared to NS.
source: Additionally, we noticed that in CHO-K1 cells in the absence of dox, mCherry expression is lower and has a wider distribution in the 5 kb reporter compared to NS (Figure 1E&I, vs. Figure 1C&G).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The observation that mCherry expression is lower in the 5 kb reporter suggests that the two promoters interfere in a distance-dependent manner.
source: This observation suggests that the two promoters interfere, as observed before (Shearwin et al., 2005), in a distance-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of lower mCherry expression in the 5 kb reporter, supported by a citation to previous literature on promoter interference.

claim: In K562, there was an increase in pRSV-mCherry expression after 5 days of dox-mediated HDAC4 recruitment and pEF-mCitrine silencing.
source: Surprisingly, in K562 we saw an increase in pRSV-mCherry expression after 5 days of dox-mediated HDAC4 recruitment and pEF-mCitrine silencing (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Transcriptional interference between pEF and pRSV results from transcriptional run-on from the pEF promoter which is resolved upon mCitrine silencing.
source: We found that this transcriptional interference between pEF and pRSV results from transcriptional run-on from the pEF promoter which is resolved upon mCitrine silencing (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A&B, Appendix 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and PCR data on cDNA shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A&B.

claim: KRAB recruitment for 5 days in K562 cells at the 5 kb reporter resulted in loss of H3Kac and a strong increase in H3K9me3 across the recruitment site, both fluorescent protein genes, and the 5 kb spacer.
source: Recruitment of KRAB for 5 days in K562 cells at the 5 kb reporter resulted in loss of the activating histone 3 lysine acetylation (H3Kac) and a strong increase in the repressive modification H3K9me3 across the recruitment site, both fluorescent protein genes, and the 5 kb spacer (Figure 2A&C).
evidence: This claim is supported by CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 2A&C.

claim: The increase in H3K9me3 and decrease in H3Kac after KRAB recruitment was also observed in the NS reporter line.
source: This increase in H3K9me3 and decrease in H3Kac was also observed in the NS reporter line (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: KRAB recruitment was accompanied by a concomitant depletion of H3K4me3 in both NS and 5 kb reporter lines.
source: and was accompanied by a concomitant depletion of histone 3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3), which is associated with active genes, in both reporter lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1&B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: An increase in H3K9me3 was observed beyond the AAVS1 integration site into neighboring genes, corresponding to a region of enrichment of approximately 50–60 kb beyond the reporter.
source: Moreover, we observed an increase in H3K9me3 beyond the AAVS1 integration site into neighboring genes (Figure 2B), corresponding to a region of enrichment of approximately 50–60 kb beyond the reporter (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C&D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C&D.

claim: The increase in H3K9me3 beyond the reporter was accompanied by a depletion of H3Kac and H3K4me3 in the immediate vicinity of the AAVS1 integration site.
source: This too was accompanied by a depletion of H3Kac and H3K4me3 in the immediate vicinity of the AAVS1 integration site.
evidence: This is stated in the text and is supported by CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar changes in chromatin modifications were observed in CHO-K1 cells after 5 days of KRAB recruitment to the 5 kb reporter.
source: We observed similar changes in chromatin modifications in CHO-K1 cells after 5 days of KRAB recruitment to the 5 kb reporter (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: HDAC4 recruitment for 5 days in CHO-K1 cells to the 5 kb and NS reporters showed a decrease in acetylation levels and no change in H3K9me3.
source: Recruitment of HDAC4 for 5 days in CHO-K1 cells to the 5 kb and NS reporters showed a decrease in acetylation levels, and no change in H3K9me3 (Figure 2D&E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B&C), as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 2D&E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B&C.

claim: H3K27me3 was detected throughout the 5 kb and the NS reporters after HDAC4 recruitment.
source: However, surprisingly histone 3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) was also detected throughout the 5 kb (Figure 2D&E) and the NS reporters (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 2D&E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: H3K27me3 is associated with polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) and not with HDAC4.
source: This repressive modification is associated with polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) and not with HDAC4.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the association of H3K27me3 with PRC2.

claim: HDAC4 recruitment at a pEF-mCitrine reporter flanked by insulators in the same locus of CHO-K1 cells does not lead to deposition of H3K27me3.
source: We have previously observed at a pEF-mCitrine reporter flanked by insulators in the same locus of CHO-K1 cells that HDAC4 recruitment does not lead to deposition of H3K27me3 (Bintu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The pRSV promoter gets silenced not by HDAC4, but by PRC2 after the pEF-mCitrine gene is silenced.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that the pRSV promoter gets silenced not by HDAC4, but by PRC2 after the pEF-mCitrine gene is silenced.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of H3K27me3 deposition and previous knowledge about PRC2.

claim: In the presence of dox and Tazemetostat (Taz), while the mCitrine gene was still silenced by HDAC4, the mCherry gene was not silenced in both the 5 kb reporter and the NS reporter.
source: We found that in the presence of dox and Taz, while the mCitrine gene was still silenced by HDAC4, the mCherry gene was not silenced (and even slightly increased in expression) in both the 5 kb reporter (Figure 2G&H) and the NS reporter (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data with EZH2 inhibitor shown in Figure 2G&H and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The silencing of mCherry is due to PRC2 action, but it can only take place once HDAC4 removes acetylation at the locus.
source: This observation suggests that silencing of the pRSV promoter is due to PRC2 action, but it can only take place once HDAC4 removes acetylation at the locus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mCherry silencing is lost upon PRC2 inhibition but mCitrine silencing is not.

claim: H3K27me3 and H3Ac are negatively correlated as measured by co-ChIP in primary cells.
source: In accordance with our hypothesis, previous studies have shown that H3K27me3 and H3Ac are negatively correlated as measured by co-ChIP in primary cells (Weiner et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lack of transcription and histone deacetylation both drive an increase in H3K27me3 deposition steadily over time.
source: that lack of transcription and histone deacetylation both drive an increase in H3K27me3 deposition steadily over time (Hosogane et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Recruitment of HDAC1 leads to repressed chromatin associated with a strong increase in H3K27me3.
source: and that recruitment of HDAC1 leads to repressed chromatin associated with a strong increase in H3K27me3 (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Knockdown of p300, a histone acetyltransferase, resulted in a global decrease of H3K27Ac in tandem with an increase in H3K27me3.
source: Additionally, knockdown of p300, a histone acetyltransferase, resulted in a global decrease of H3K27Ac in tandem with an increase in H3K27me3 (Martire et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Upon KRAB recruitment, only a slight delay of 2.3 ± 3.1 hr was observed between mCitrine and mCherry silencing in the NS reporter.
source: Upon KRAB recruitment, we observed only a slight delay of 2.3 ± 3.1 hr between mCitrine and mCherry silencing in the NS reporter
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3B&C.

claim: Upon KRAB recruitment, a longer delay of 12.3 ± 9.8 hr was observed between mCitrine and mCherry silencing in the 5 kb reporter.
source: and a longer delay of 12.3 ± 9.8 hr in the 5 kb reporter (Figure 3B&C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A&B).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3B&C.

claim: Spreading of HDAC4-mediated transcriptional silencing was slower, and no appreciable difference in silencing delays was observed between NS and 5 kb reporter lines.
source: In contrast, spreading of HDAC4-mediated transcriptional silencing was slower, and no appreciable difference in silencing delays was observed between reporter lines (NS: 37 ±21 hr; 5 kb: 32 ±19 hr) (Figure 3D&E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C&D).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3D&E.

claim: KRAB-mediated spreading of transcriptional silencing is distance-dependent in CHO-K1 cells.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that KRAB-mediated spreading of transcriptional silencing is distance-dependent in CHO-K1 cells
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the delay between mCitrine and mCherry silencing increases with distance for KRAB.

claim: HDAC4 mediated spreading is distance-independent at these length scales.
source: while HDAC4 mediated spreading is distance-independent at these length scales.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the delay between mCitrine and mCherry silencing does not change with distance for HDAC4.

claim: KRAB recruitment results in silencing delays that increase with intergenic distance in CHO-K1 and K562 cells.
source: KRAB recruitment results in silencing delays that increase with intergenic distance (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry model fits shown in Figure 3I.

claim: HDAC4 recruitment results in delays that are not statistically different among different distances in either CHO-K1 or K562 cell types.
source: HDAC4 recruitment results in delays that are not statistically different among different distances in either cell type
evidence: This is stated in the text and is supported by flow cytometry model fits shown in Figure 3J.

claim: HDAC4 recruitment shows a trend where delay decreases with increased distance in K562 from around 10 days in the NS reporter to around 5 days in the 5 kb reporter.
source: but show a trend where delay decreases with increased distance in K562 from around 10 days in the NS reporter to around 5 days in the 5 kb reporter (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry model fits shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Silencing spreads slower in K562 versus CHO-K1 cells after both KRAB and HDAC4 recruitment.
source: Silencing spreads slower in K562 versus CHO-K1 cells after both KRAB and HDAC4 recruitment (Figure 3I&J)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry model fits shown in Figure 3I&J.

claim: The pRSV promoter is stronger in K562 cells, as indicated by higher mCherry expression compared to CHO-K1 cells for both the NS and 5 kb reporters.
source: This is most likely because the pRSV promoter is stronger in K562 cells, as indicated by higher mCherry expression compared to CHO-K1 cells for both the NS and 5 kb reporters (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: No cHS4 insulator configuration was capable of stopping KRAB-mediated spreading of silencing in either CHO-K1 or K562 cells.
source: Surprisingly, no cHS4 insulator configuration was capable of stopping KRAB-mediated spreading of silencing in either CHO-K1 or K562 cells (Figure 4C&D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A&B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C&D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A&B.

claim: cHS4 insulators do not delay KRAB-mediated silencing: the estimated delay times in the insulator reporters are close to the delays in reporters with spacers.
source: Moreover, cHS4 insulators do not delay KRAB-mediated silencing either: the estimated delay times in the insulator reporters are close to the delays in reporters with spacers (Figure 4F, Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry model fits shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In CHO-K1 cells, no cHS4 insulator configuration was able to inhibit spreading of silencing upon HDAC4 recruitment.
source: In CHO-K1 cells, no cHS4 insulator configuration was able to inhibit spreading of silencing upon HDAC4 recruitment (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: cHS4 insulators do appear to attenuate HDAC4-mediated mCherry silencing in K562 cells, even with 20 days of recruitment.
source: However, cHS4 insulators do appear to attenuate HDAC4-mediated mCherry silencing in K562 cells, even with 20 days of recruitment (Figure 4G&H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4G&H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In K562, a broadening of the mCherry fluorescence distribution was seen with the majority of cells expressing lower levels of mCherry than the population without dox, both at 5 and 20 days of HDAC4 recruitment to cHS4 insulator constructs.
source: Rather than seeing complete silencing of the mCherry reporter, we see a broadening of the mCherry fluorescence distribution with the majority of cells expressing lower levels of mCherry than the population without dox, both at 5 and 20 days of HDAC4 recruitment to cHS4 insulator constructs in K562 (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the DC configuration, the mCherry distribution remains in the ON range even after 20 days of HDAC4 recruitment.
source: An exception to this observation is the DC configuration, where the mCherry distribution remains in the ON range even after 20 days of HDAC4 recruitment (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: At lower dox concentrations, silencing delay times decrease upon increasing dox concentrations for all cHS4 insulator configurations.
source: At lower levels of dox, silencing of the two genes is slower; fits of daily flow cytometry data show silencing delay times that decrease upon increasing dox concentrations for all cHS4 insulator configurations (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry model fits shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: At lower dox concentrations, fewer cells silence mCitrine by the end of 5 days, but those that do are likely to also silence mCherry for both HDAC4 and KRAB.
source: At lower dox concentrations, fewer cells silence mCitrine by the end of 5 days, but those that do are likely to also silence mCherry for both HDAC4 and KRAB (Figure 4—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The cHS4 insulators are able to prevent spontaneous background silencing of the reporters in the absence of dox in CHO-K1 cells.
source: Although the cHS4 insulators do not generally prevent spreading of silencing during recruitment of CRs, the insulators are able to prevent spontaneous background silencing of the reporters in the absence of dox in CHO-K1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5, Appendix 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Levels of mCherry expression are higher in the cHS4 insulator constructs.
source: Overall, levels of mCherry expression are higher in the cHS4 insulator constructs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is no transcriptional run-on mRNA across the SH insulator.
source: and there is no transcriptional run-on mRNA across the SH insulator (Appendix 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 4E&F)
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data on cDNA shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4E&F.

claim: In CHO-K1 cells, both genes reactivated simultaneously in the NS reporter after release of KRAB or HDAC4.
source: In CHO-K1 cells, while both genes reactivated simultaneously in the NS reporter (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A&B)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A&B.

claim: In CHO-K1 cells, mCitrine reactivated first in the 5 kb reporter after release of KRAB or HDAC4.
source: mCitrine reactivated first in the 5 kb reporter (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C&D), both after release of KRAB or HDAC4.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C&D.

claim: The pattern of a distance-dependent delay in reactivation between mCitrine and mCherry holds for the insulator configurations for both KRAB and HDAC4 in CHO-K1 cells.
source: This pattern of a distance-dependent delay in reactivation between mCitrine and mCherry also holds for the insulator configurations for both KRAB and HDAC4: the full 1.2 kb long cHS4 configurations featured delayed mCherry reactivation (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), compared to the more synchronous reactivation patterns observed in the 250 bp long core insulator configurations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In CHO-K1 cells, reactivation initiates at the stronger pEF promoter that drives mCitrine, and spreads in a distance-dependent manner to the weaker pRSV-mCherry gene.
source: The order of reactivation suggests that in CHO-K1 cells reactivation initiates at the stronger pEF promoter that drives mCitrine, and spreads in a distance-dependent manner to the weaker pRSV-mCherry gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mCitrine reactivates first in the 5 kb reporter and that reactivation is distance-dependent.

claim: In K562 cells after release of KRAB, for the NS reporter, mCherry reactivates first.
source: However, when looking at order of reactivation in K562 cells after release of KRAB, we found that for the NS reporter, mCherry reactivates first (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: In K562 cells with the 5 kb reporter after release of KRAB, three different scenarios are observed in individual cells: either mCherry reactivates first, mCitrine reactivates first, or they reactivate together.
source: while with the 5 kb reporter we observe three different scenarios in individual cells: either mCherry reactivates first, mCitrine reactivates first, or they reactivate together (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In the cHS4 insulator constructs in K562 cells, mCherry reactivates before mCitrine after release of KRAB.
source: In the cHS4 insulator constructs, mCherry reactivates before mCitrine in K562 cells (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The change in reactivation pattern in K562 cells compared to CHO-K1 is likely due to the pRSV promoter being stronger in K562.
source: This change in reactivation pattern in K562 cells compared to CHO-K1 is likely due to the pRSV promoter being stronger in K562 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that reactivation order differs between cell types and that pRSV expression is higher in K562.

claim: After release of rTetR-KRAB, reporters with insulators reactivated more rapidly compared to the NS and 5 kb reporters in both CHO-K1 and K562 cells.
source: After release of rTetR-KRAB, reporters with insulators reactivated more rapidly compared to the NS and 5 kb reporters, with the double core insulator exhibiting the highest degree of gene reactivation in both CHO-K1 and K562 cells (Figure 5H&I).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5H&I.

claim: The extent of epigenetic memory in the system depends on the chromatin regulator recruited and the configurations of promoters and insulators at the target locus.
source: These results show that the extent of epigenetic memory in our system depends on the chromatin regulator recruited and the configurations of promoters and insulators at the target locus, with the stronger pEF promoter closely surrounded by cHS4 insulators diminishing memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that reactivation dynamics vary with CR type, promoter strength, and insulator presence.

claim: When KRAB is recruited upstream of pEF-mCitrine, silencing of the downstream pRSV-mCherry gene happens quickly (over hours) at a rate that decreases as the distance between pRSV-mCherry and pEF-mCitrine increases.
source: When KRAB is recruited upstream of pEF-mCitrine, silencing of the downstream pRSV-mCherry gene happens quickly (over hours) at a rate that decreases as the distance between pRSV-mCherry and pEF-mCitrine increases (Figure 6B, ks_KRAB(d))
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: When HDAC4 is recruited upstream of pEF-mCitrine, delayed silencing of pRSV-mCherry (over many days, compared to hours in KRAB) is observed at a rate that does not change as a function of the distance between the two genes.
source: However, when HDAC4 is recruited upstream of pEF-mCitrine, we observe delayed silencing of pRSV-mCherry (over many days, compared to hours in KRAB) at a rate that does not change as a function of the distance between the two genes.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: pRSV-mCherry silencing after HDAC4 recruitment is not due to the direct action of the HDACs recruited upstream of the pEF, but rather due to background silencing of pRSV by endogenous polycomb complexes.
source: We hypothesize that pRSV-mCherry silencing is not due to the direct action of the HDACs recruited upstream of the pEF, but rather due to background silencing (Figure 6C, kbs2 ) of pRSV by endogenous polycomb complexes as indicated by the appearance of H3K27me3 (Figure 2D&E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B&C), loss of pRSV-mCherry silencing upon PRC2 inhibition (Figure 2G–H), and the fact that the silencing delay is distance-independent.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple lines of evidence including CUT&RUN data and EZH2 inhibitor experiments.

claim: The pRSV promoter is more prone to transgene background silencing than the pEF promoter when integrated into mammalian genomes.
source: In line with our hypothesis, previous studies have shown that the pRSV promoter is more prone to transgene background silencing than the pEF promoter when integrated into mammalian genomes (Garrison et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: When pEF is active, it can increase activity of the downstream pRSV and prevent it from background silencing.
source: Because we see much less pRSV-mCherry background silencing when the upstream pEF- mCitrine is active (in the absence of dox), we conclude that when pEF is active, it can increase activity of the downstream pRSV and prevent it from background silencing (Figure 6D, ka1(d)).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that background silencing of pRSV is reduced when pEF is active.

claim: Once the pEF-mCitrine gene is silenced by HDAC4, it can no longer bolster the overall rate of reactivation at the pRSV-mCherry gene and protect it against background silencing.
source: Once the pEF-mCitrine gene is silenced by HDAC4, it can no longer bolster the overall rate of reactivation at the pRSV-mCherry gene (ka1(d) is missing in Figure 6C compared to 6D) and protect it against background silencing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and the observation that pRSV silencing occurs after pEF silencing.

claim: In the system, both silencing and reactivation rates are affected by the distance between two genes.
source: In summary, in our system both silencing and reactivation rates are affected by the distance between two genes.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upon recruitment of KRAB, a CR associated with reader-writer feedback and spreading of silencing histone modifications, the silencing rate is maximal near its recruitment sites and decreases slowly with distance.
source: Upon recruitment of KRAB, a CR associated with reader-writer feedback and spreading of silencing histone modifications, the silencing rate is maximal near its recruitment sites and decreases slowly with distance (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings and the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: HDAC4 recruitment leads to histone deacetylation, which is not associated with reader-writer positive feedback, and therefore is expected to decrease quickly over distance.
source: However, HDAC4 recruitment leads to histone deacetylation, which is not associated with reader-writer positive feedback, and therefore is expected to decrease quickly over distance (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism of HDAC4 action and the experimental findings.

claim: CRs that are associated with positive reader-writer feedback loops can directly affect nearby genes, while CRs without feedback can only indirectly affect neighboring genes by changing the state of promoters very close to the recruitment site.
source: We hypothesize that CRs that are associated with positive reader-writer feedback loops can directly affect nearby genes, while CRs without feedback can only indirectly affect neighboring genes by changing the state of promoters very close to the recruitment site, which can in turn influence farther genes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings and the model.

claim: In the absence of chromatin regulator recruitment, each gene drives its own activation and in addition drives the reactivation of the neighboring gene in a distance-dependent manner.
source: In the absence of chromatin regulator recruitment, each gene drives its own activation and in addition drives the reactivation of the neighboring gene in a distance-dependent manner (Figure 6F, top).
evidence: This is a component of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: In CHO-K1 cells, the pEF is a stronger promoter than the pRSV, while in K562 their strengths are closer.
source: In CHO-K1 cells, the pEF is a stronger promoter than the pRSV, while in K562 their strengths are closer (Figure 6F bottom, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of different expression levels and reactivation patterns in the two cell types.

claim: When a gene is silent, the promoter can only reactivate itself and has no effect on reactivation of the adjacent gene until it is active again.
source: However, when a gene is silent, we are led to assume that the promoter can only reactivate itself and has no effect on reactivation of the adjacent gene until it is active again (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is an assumption made in the model to explain the experimental observations.

claim: The core region of the cHS4 insulator can increase the rate of reactivation of nearby genes in a distance-dependent manner.
source: Similar to promoters, the core region of the cHS4 insulator can be modeled as a DNA element that increases the rate of reactivation of nearby genes in our setup in a distance-dependent manner (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a component of the model presented in the manuscript, based on the experimental observations.

claim: Insulators can prevent background gene silencing and drive reactivation after targeted CR-mediated silencing.
source: This action, combined with our promoter reactivation rates, can prevent background gene silencing (Figure 6D) and drive reactivation after targeted CR-mediated silencing (Figure 6B&C).
evidence: This is a component of the model presented in the manuscript, based on the experimental observations.

source: For example, because insulators increase reactivation rates, they can fight background silencing of the pRSV-mCherry both upon HDAC4 recruitment (Figure 6C), and under conditions without dox (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a component of the model presented in the manuscript, based on the experimental observations.

claim: In K562, where the rate associated with pRSV activation is higher than in CHO-K1, the core insulators can bring the overall activation rate above background silencing when they are closer to pRSV.
source: In K562, where the rate associated with pRSV activation is higher than in CHO-K1, the core insulators can bring the overall activation rate above background silencing when they are closer to pRSV.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and the experimental observations.

claim: Because the activation rates associated with insulators are small compared to KRAB-mediated silencing rates, they cannot insulate well against KRAB.
source: However, because the activation rates associated with insulators are small compared to KRAB-mediated silencing rates, they cannot insulate well against KRAB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and the experimental observations.

claim: In CHO-K1 cells, the stronger pEF gene and presence of any insulators leads to the reactivation of the mCitrine gene, which then can act at a distance to help reactivate the weaker pRSV-mCherry gene.
source: In CHO-K1 cells, the stronger pEF gene and presence of any insulators leads to the reactivation of the mCitrine gene, which then can act at a distance to help reactivate the weaker pRSV-mCherry gene (Figure 6I, left).
evidence: This is a component of the model presented in the manuscript, based on the experimental observations.

evidence: This is a component of the model presented in the manuscript, based on the experimental observations.
